implementation_notes: kotlinx.coroutines Channel<E> is the suspending typed channel: Channel<Order>() with send/receive replaces BlockingQueue, the element type is the channel contract, and the capacity constants (Channel.RENDEZVOUS, CONFLATED, UNLIMITED, BUFFERED) plus onBufferOverflow make each type's back-pressure policy explicit instead of accidental. Where the channel is a broadcast rather than a hand-off - many consumers, no per-element acknowledgement - the library's intended replacement is a hot MutableSharedFlow<Order>, which keeps the per-type binding while giving up the queue semantics; the shared flow is never closed and drops emissions when no subscriber is present. Both forms get cancellation and shutdown from the coroutine Job/scope that owns them, and onUndeliveredElement is the correct hook for releasing per-type resources.
code_sketch:
val orders = Channel<Order>(capacity = 1000, onBufferOverflow = BufferOverflow.SUSPEND)

launch { while (true) handle(orders.receive()) }   // consumer owns exactly one type
orders.send(order)                                // suspends when the buffer is full

// broadcast instead of hand-off:
val events = MutableSharedFlow<OrderEvent>(extraBufferCapacity = 64)
pitfalls: Channel is a hand-off, not a broadcast: two consumers of the same Channel split the messages instead of both seeing them; use SharedFlow for fan-out, and expect it to drop emissions when nobody collects.

The prompt cancellation guarantee means an element can be extracted from the channel and still be lost when the receiver coroutine is cancelled in parallel; use onUndeliveredElement to release whatever the element owns.
An unlimited or oversized buffer hides a slow consumer rather than applying backpressure, so the type keeps its latency but loses its memory predictability.

variants.name: MutableSharedFlow<Order> (hot broadcast per message type)
variants.implementation_notes: The reactive sibling per type: a hot flow broadcasts every emission to all current subscribers, so the channel identity is still the type parameter while the delivery semantics become pub-sub instead of hand-off. It is the documented replacement for BroadcastChannel, supports replay and extraBufferCapacity for slow subscribers, and never completes - errors and completion must be materialized as values if consumers need them. Choose it when several components must observe the same per-type stream; choose Channel when each message must be processed exactly once.
pitfalls: A shared flow has no completion and no failure channel: closing semantics and errors must be modelled explicitly, unlike a Channel that can be closed.
Emissions with no subscriber are lost (replay = 0), so a consumer that starts late silently misses the type's earlier messages.
